Use the order-topology interval basis and a sandwich argument.

For the first conjunct, reduce continuity at \(a\) to controlling \(f\) inside an arbitrary interval neighborhood of \(f(a)\). Since \(f(s)\) is a neighborhood of \(f(a)\), density of \(\beta\) supplies image points \(f(x_-)\) and \(f(x_+)\) lying sufficiently close below and above \(f(a)\), still inside that interval. As \(s\) is a neighborhood of \(a\), \(a,x_-,x_+\in s\); strict monotonicity then gives
\[
x_-<a<x_+.
\]
Every \(x\in s\cap(x_-,x_+)\) is consequently mapped between \(f(x_-)\) and \(f(x_+)\). This produces a neighborhood of \(a\) mapped into the prescribed neighborhood of \(f(a)\).

For the second conjunct, use the one-sided interval basis on \(Iic\,a\). Monotonicity already gives the upper bound
\[
x\le a \implies f(x)\le f(a).
\]
The hypothesis that \(f(s)\) is a neighborhood of \(f(a)\) within \(Iic(f(a))\), together with density, supplies a suitable image point \(f(x_-)\) just below \(f(a)\). Then monotonicity sandwiches every \(x\in s\cap Iic(a)\) sufficiently close to \(a\):
\[
f(x_-)\le f(x)\le f(a).
\]
Thus a left-neighborhood of \(a\) maps into any prescribed left-neighborhood of \(f(a)\).

Endpoint cases should be discharged using the standard order-topology neighborhood-basis lemmas; density of \(\beta\) is the essential assumption ensuring that nontrivial comparison points can be chosen when needed.
